mcqs.question: Why does LRU Cache's O(1) get/put contract require combining a hashmap with a doubly linked list, rather than using either alone?
options: A hashmap alone can track recency order but lacks O(1) lookup
A doubly linked list alone gives O(1) lookup but no way to track recency
A hashmap gives O(1) lookup but no recency tracking, and a doubly linked list gives O(1) recency reordering but O(n) lookup — pairing them lets each cover the other's gap
Neither structure can achieve O(1) time for get or put under any combination
mcqs.explanation: Each structure is missing exactly what the other provides: the hashmap skips the list's linear search, and the list gives ordering the hashmap has no concept of. The first two options have the trade-offs backwards.

mcqs.question: Why does LRU Cache specifically need a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?
options: A singly linked list already supports O(1) removal given just a node reference
Doubly linked lists are only needed once the cache capacity exceeds a fixed threshold
A doubly linked list uses less memory per node than a singly linked list
Removing an arbitrary node in O(1) needs a back-pointer to redirect the previous node's next, which only a doubly linked list provides directly
mcqs.explanation: A singly linked list has no way to reach the previous node from a given node reference, so unlinking it in O(1) is impossible without a back-pointer — exactly what a doubly linked list adds. Doubly linked nodes use more memory per node, not less, due to the extra pointer.

mcqs.question: Why does get(key) run in O(1) even though it both looks up a key and reorders the linked list?
options: The hashmap eliminates the O(n) search for the node, and moving that node to the front costs O(1) since the doubly linked list needs no traversal to unlink an already-located node
get() only touches the hashmap; the linked list is exclusively used by put()
Moving a node to the front requires re-hashing its key each time
get() runs in O(log n) because the hashmap must resolve a collision chain
mcqs.explanation: Both steps are O(1): the hashmap jumps straight to the node, and the doubly linked list's back-pointer lets it unlink and reinsert that node without scanning anything. get() does use the linked list, and no re-hashing happens on reorder.

mcqs.question: Why must LRU Cache eviction update both the doubly linked list and the hashmap, rather than just one of them?
options: Removing a node from the list alone is sufficient; the map self-corrects on the next access
Deleting the map entry alone is sufficient; the list node is garbage collected automatically
Eviction requires unlinking the node from the list and deleting its hashmap entry — skipping either produces a stale hit or an orphaned, memory-wasting node
Eviction only requires updating the hashmap because the list is rebuilt from the map on every put
mcqs.explanation: The two structures are only correct in sync — an unlinked-but-still-mapped node returns a stale value, and a deleted-but-still-linked node wastes memory and corrupts recency order. Neither structure self-corrects, and the list is never rebuilt from the map.

mcqs.question: What extra bookkeeping does LFU (Least Frequently Used) eviction need compared to LRU?
options: LFU has strictly better time complexity than LRU for both get and put
LFU needs an additional map from frequency count to a list of keys at that frequency, plus tracking the current minimum frequency — genuinely more bookkeeping than LRU's single list
LRU and LFU are mathematically equivalent eviction policies
LFU requires no additional data structures beyond what LRU already uses
mcqs.explanation: LFU has to jump straight to the lowest-frequency bucket on eviction, which needs a frequency-to-keys map and a tracked minimum frequency — LRU's single doubly linked list has no equivalent. Both achieve O(1), and the two policies evict on genuinely different criteria.

mcqs.question: You implement LRU Cache using Python's OrderedDict in an interview. Why might that answer fall short even though it's correct and O(1)?
options: OrderedDict cannot achieve O(1) get/put, making it unsuitable for LRU Cache
OrderedDict uses a completely different, unrelated mechanism from a hashmap plus linked list
move_to_end and popitem(last=False) are both O(n) operations internally
OrderedDict already implements a hashmap-plus-doubly-linked-list internally, but reaching for it without being able to explain that mechanism misses what the question is actually testing
mcqs.explanation: OrderedDict is a fine production choice, but an interviewer asking you to design LRU Cache wants to see the hashmap-and-linked-list mechanism itself, which the built-in hides. It is O(1) for both operations and is built on essentially the same underlying idea, not something unrelated.
